name: Khopra Danda
tagline: A community lodge on a 3,660 m ridge facing Dhaulagiri
meta_description: Khopra Danda (3,660 m) above Ghorepani: community lodge, Dhaulagiri and Annapurna South views, Khayer Lake day hike, routes, best months and costs.
summary: Khopra Danda is a grassy ridge at 3,660 m west of Ghorepani, crowned by a community-run lodge with a front-row view of Dhaulagiri at 8,167 m and the Annapurna South massif. It is reached in 2–3 days from the Poon Hill trail and makes a quieter, higher alternative to Poon Hill.
intro: Khopra Danda, danda meaning ridge in Nepali, is a long shoulder of yak pasture that rises above the Kali Gandaki side of the Annapurna foothills. At 3,660 m it is about 450 m higher than Poon Hill, and instead of looking at the mountains from a crowded tower, you sleep on the ridge and watch the light change across Dhaulagiri, Tukuche Peak, Nilgiri, Annapurna South and Fang from the lodge door. It is one of the best viewpoints in the region that most visitors have never heard of.

The trail was developed in the 2000s as a community trekking route, and the lodges at Khopra and on the way, at Chistibang and Bayeli, were built to bring income to the Magar and Gurung villages below, especially Swanta and Paudwar. The lodge at Khopra is simple: dormitories, a few private rooms, a warm dining room and solar power. In return you get silence after dark, an enormous sky and few other trekkers outside the peak weeks of October.

Above the ridge, a further climb leads to Khayer Lake, also written Kaire, at about 4,660 m, a small glacial lake under Annapurna South that is sacred to Hindus. Pilgrims walk up to bathe in it around Janai Purnima in August. For trekkers it is a long, demanding day hike from Khopra, with the Annapurna South glaciers hanging directly above. Khopra links easily with Ghorepani and Poon Hill, so most itineraries combine both in 7–11 days from Pokhara.
facts: Dhaulagiri views, community lodge, Khayer Lake

highlights.title: Dhaulagiri across the Kali Gandaki
highlights.text: Dhaulagiri I, at 8,167 m the seventh-highest mountain on Earth, stands directly west of the ridge, with the deep Kali Gandaki gorge between. At sunset its huge south face goes from white to gold to pink, and the lodge terrace is the best seat. Tukuche Peak and Dhaulagiri II to VI line up beside it.

highlights.title: Annapurna South and Fang overhead
highlights.text: Turn north-east and Annapurna South at 7,219 m and its neighbour Fang, or Baraha Shikhar, fill the sky above the pastures. Their glaciers feed the streams that run past the lodge. Nilgiri and the peaks above Jomsom close the view to the north, a panorama that Poon Hill only shows from a distance.

highlights.title: Khayer Lake, a sacred high lake
highlights.text: A long day hike from Khopra climbs about 1,000 m to Khayer Lake at around 4,660 m, beneath the ice of Annapurna South. Hindu pilgrims visit at Janai Purnima in August to bathe and make offerings. For trekkers it is the highest point of the region's lodge treks, demanding 8–9 hours there and back.

highlights.title: Community lodges that fund villages
highlights.text: The lodges at Khopra, Chistibang and Bayeli were set up as community enterprises, with income supporting schools and health services in villages like Swanta and Paudwar. Staff rotate from those villages. Food is simple and portions generous, and your spending here stays in the local economy more directly than on busier trails.

highlights.title: Night skies without light pollution
highlights.text: With no road, no village and only solar lights on the ridge, the sky over Khopra on a clear autumn night is dark enough to see the Milky Way rise behind Annapurna South. Photographers bring tripods for star trails; everyone else steps out after dinner, wrapped in a down jacket, for ten minutes of stars.

highlights.title: Yak and sheep pastures
highlights.text: In summer and autumn, herders from the lower villages graze yak, cows and sheep on the high pastures around Khopra and Bayeli. You may pass their stone shelters and smell the smoke of their fires, and the Swanta area has a small yak cheese making tradition that you can sample on the way down.

how_to_reach.text: Drive from Pokhara to Ghandruk in about 3 hours, or to Hile and Ulleri in 2.5–3.5 hours, depending on which direction you walk the loop. Kathmandu to Pokhara is about 200 km and 6–8 hours by road.

Two main routes. From Tadapani at 2,630 m: Dobato at about 3,420 m, then Bayeli Kharka and Khopra, 2 days. From Ghorepani at 2,874 m: down to Swanta at 2,214 m, up to Chistibang at 3,026 m and on to Khopra, 2–3 days. Many treks go up one way and down the other.

There is no scheduled helicopter service. In an emergency, helicopters can land on the open ridge near the lodge in good weather; evacuation to Pokhara takes about 20 minutes in the air. This is why we require insurance that covers helicopter rescue up to at least 5,000 m.

where_to_stay: Accommodation on the ridge is the community lodge at Khopra, with dormitories of four to eight beds, a handful of twin rooms and a shared dining hall with a stove. Toilets are shared and showers are limited, especially when it is cold. Below the ridge, Chistibang at 3,026 m and Bayeli Kharka have similar small community lodges, and Swanta has a few family teahouses. In peak October weeks the twin rooms book out, so we reserve ahead and warn guests that a dorm night is possible. Bring a sleeping bag rated to −10 °C.
tips: Spend two nights on the ridge so that a cloudy evening does not cost you the Dhaulagiri view.
Start the Khayer Lake hike before 6 am, as cloud often builds over Annapurna South by midday.
Carry cash in Nepali rupees, because the community lodge cannot take cards and there are no ATMs beyond Pokhara.
Pack a power bank: solar charging at Khopra is limited and slow on cloudy days.
Do not attempt the Khopra ridge without a guide in winter, when snow hides the trail above Bayeli and Chistibang.

experiences.title: Khayer Lake day hike from Khopra
experiences.summary: A demanding day hike from Khopra Danda to Khayer Lake at about 4,660 m, a small sacred lake at the foot of Annapurna South's glaciers. Expect roughly 1,000 m of ascent, 8–9 hours of walking and the highest point of the Khopra trek.
body: We leave Khopra at first light with packed breakfast and lunch. The trail climbs north-east across open pasture, then into a rocky ablation valley below the glaciers of Annapurna South. Height gain is roughly 1,000 m to the lake, and the path is faint in places, with boulder sections that need care. Without a guide who knows the route, it is easy to lose time on the wrong side of the valley.

Khayer Lake, also spelled Kaire or Khayar, lies at about 4,660 m and is sacred to Hindus, who associate it with the goddess Barahi. Each August around Janai Purnima, pilgrims from the Myagdi villages walk up to bathe in its cold water and make offerings. Outside that season the lake is usually deserted, with a few prayer flags and small shrines. The ice walls of Annapurna South rise close above, and you can hear seracs crack in the afternoon.

Because the lake sits nearly 1,000 m above your previous night's sleep, the hike is a good acclimatisation test. Anyone with a bad headache or nausea should turn back early. Cloud often builds over the glaciers by late morning, so we aim to reach the lake by about 11 am. The descent back to the Khopra lodge takes 3–4 hours, and a hot dinner and early bed follow. Walking poles help on the long return over loose moraine.

faqs.q: How difficult is the Khayer Lake hike?
faqs.a: It is the hardest day on any Khopra itinerary: about 1,000 m of climbing to roughly 4,660 m and 8–9 hours of walking in total, partly on faint trails and boulders. You need good fitness and should feel well acclimatised after a night at Khopra. It is optional on our treks; anyone who prefers can rest on the ridge instead.

faqs.q: Is Khayer Lake a pilgrimage site?
faqs.a: Yes. Khayer Lake is sacred to Hindus in the Myagdi and Kaski area, who associate it with the goddess Barahi. The main pilgrimage happens around Janai Purnima, usually in August, when devotees walk up to bathe and make offerings. Visitors should not swim, wash with soap or leave rubbish near the shrines at any time of year.

faqs.q: Can you camp at Khayer Lake?
faqs.a: There are no lodges at the lake, and camping requires full equipment carried up from Khopra, plus extra care at around 4,660 m, where sleeping without prior acclimatisation is risky. Almost every trekker visits as a day hike from the Khopra community lodge. We can arrange a camping extension for experienced, well-acclimatised groups on request.

experiences.title: Sunset on Dhaulagiri from the Khopra ridge
experiences.summary: From the grassy crest above the Khopra lodge, Dhaulagiri's 8,167 m south face catches the last light of the day across the Kali Gandaki gorge. On clear autumn and winter evenings it is the main event of any stay on the ridge.
body: Most groups reach Khopra in the early afternoon, drop their bags and climb ten minutes above the lodge to a small knoll with prayer flags. From here the whole western horizon opens: Dhaulagiri I in the centre, its satellites II to VI stepping away to the left, and Tukuche Peak and the Dhampus Pass area to the right. Between you and them the Kali Gandaki has cut one of the deepest gorges on Earth.

In October and November the sun sets around 5:30 pm, and the show starts about 45 minutes before. The snow goes from white to cream, then to deep gold, and finally a short pink glow lingers on the summit after the valley has gone dark. Turn around and Annapurna South, behind you, turns orange too. Bring a warm jacket, as temperatures drop below freezing within minutes of the sun leaving the ridge.

Photographers should use a tripod and a telephoto lens of 100–300 mm to isolate the Dhaulagiri summit, and a wider lens for the panorama with the lodge and prayer flags in the foreground. Clouds rising from the Kali Gandaki often add drama, but they can also hide the peak entirely, which is why we always plan two nights on the ridge. Batteries drain fast in the cold, so keep a spare in an inside pocket and swap it in just before the light peaks.

faqs.q: Is the view from Khopra better than Poon Hill?
faqs.a: For Dhaulagiri, yes. Khopra is 450 m higher and closer to both Dhaulagiri and Annapurna South, and you watch sunset and sunrise from your lodge instead of joining hundreds of people on a tower. Poon Hill has the easier access and a wider spread of peaks to the east. Many treks visit both, with Poon Hill on one morning and Khopra for two evenings.

faqs.q: What time is sunset at Khopra Danda?
faqs.a: In October sunset is around 5:45 pm, moving to about 5:15 pm by late November and early December. The best colour on Dhaulagiri comes in the 30–40 minutes before the sun drops below the horizon, followed by a short alpenglow. Be on the knoll above the lodge by 4:45 pm in autumn to catch the whole sequence.

faqs.q: Can I see Dhaulagiri from Khopra in spring?
faqs.a: Often, but less reliably than in autumn. In March and April the mornings are usually clear, while afternoon haze and cloud build over the Kali Gandaki, so the sunset can be hidden. Plan to watch at dawn as well. In May, dust and pre-monsoon cloud make long views less predictable still, though the rhododendrons below the ridge are in flower.

experiences.title: Swanta village and yak cheese on the way down
experiences.summary: Descending from Khopra to Swanta at 2,214 m, the trail passes summer pastures and drops into a Magar farming village with a small tradition of yak and cow cheese making. A good place for a slow lunch and a look at hill farm life.
body: The trail from Khopra to Swanta loses around 1,450 m in 4–5 hours, first across open grazing land, then down through rhododendron and oak forest to the terraced fields above the village. In the herding season you pass shelters where families from the lower villages spend summer and autumn with their animals, making butter and cheese and drying it on racks inside. Watch your footing on the steeper forest sections, which stay damp in the shade.

Swanta is a Magar village of stone houses and kitchen gardens on the slopes above the Myagdi side. A few households run small lodges, and the area is known among trekkers for its cheese, made from yak and cow milk. It is not a factory: production is small and seasonal, and what is available depends on the time of year. Your guide can ask around and arrange a tasting with tea in one of the lodges.

From Swanta, the trail climbs about 660 m back to Ghorepani in around 4 hours, reconnecting with the main Poon Hill circuit. Many trekkers spend the night in Swanta to break the descent, which also gives you an evening in a village that sees far fewer visitors than Ghorepani. The dal bhat here is cooked with home-grown vegetables and is among the best on the route. Rooms are simple and the evening is quiet, with the lights of the Myagdi villages below.

faqs.q: Where is Swanta on the Khopra trek?
faqs.a: Swanta is a Magar village at about 2,214 m on the slopes south-west of Ghorepani. On a loop through Khopra it is either your first stop after leaving Ghorepani or your last before returning there. It is about 4–5 hours below Khopra and 4 hours from Ghorepani, so it splits the route neatly into manageable days.

faqs.q: Can vegetarians eat well on the Khopra trek?
faqs.a: Yes, very well. Dal bhat with lentils, rice, vegetable curry and greens is available at every lodge and refilled without extra charge. Swanta's cheese and potatoes add variety. Meat is rarely on the menu on the ridge and is often not fresh when it is, so many trekkers, not only vegetarians, stick to vegetarian food above Swanta.

faqs.q: Is Swanta cheese available all year?
faqs.a: No. Cheese making is small-scale and depends on the herding season and how much milk the animals give, so supply varies through the year and between years. Late summer and autumn are usually best. If none is available, the village lodges still serve good potatoes, fresh vegetables and buckwheat bread instead.

Khopra Danda is at about 3,660 m, roughly 450 m higher than Poon Hill at 3,210 m. Khayer Lake, the optional day hike above it, lies at around 4,660 m. Sleeping at 3,660 m can cause mild altitude symptoms, so we approach over two or three days from Ghorepani or Tadapani rather than in a single big climb.

faqs.q: How many days is the Khopra Danda trek?
faqs.a: Most itineraries take 6–8 days from Pokhara, including Ghorepani and Poon Hill. Our standard Khopra trek is 8 days with a spare day for Khayer Lake; our photography trek is 11 days with three nights on the ridge. A short version of 5–6 days is possible if you skip the lake and drive both ways.

faqs.q: Is the Khopra Danda trek hard?
faqs.a: It is a Moderate trek with daily walks of 4–6 hours and a few steep sections, particularly the climb from Swanta to Chistibang and the descent back down. The Khayer Lake hike, if you include it, is a hard day. Anyone who can manage Poon Hill comfortably and walks regularly at home can do Khopra.

faqs.q: Khopra Danda or Poon Hill, which should I choose?
faqs.a: Poon Hill suits a short 4-day trip and first-time trekkers; it is lower, busier and has more comfortable teahouses. Khopra suits people with a week or more who want a quieter trail, a higher viewpoint and the chance to sleep in front of Dhaulagiri. The best answer is often both: Poon Hill one morning, then on to Khopra.

faqs.q: What permits do I need for Khopra Danda?
faqs.a: You need an ACAP permit, which costs NPR 3,000 for foreigners and NPR 1,000 for SAARC nationals including Indians. Since 2023 Nepal's rules have required foreign trekkers in conservation areas to walk with a licensed guide; enforcement has varied, and the route is easy to lose above the tree line anyway. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the accommodation like at Khopra?
faqs.a: Simple. The community lodge has dormitories, a few twin rooms, shared toilets and a stove-heated dining room. Solar power runs the lights and limited charging. Hot showers are not always possible in cold weather. It is clean and friendly, and the view from the door makes up for the basics, but bring a warm sleeping bag.

faqs.q: Can I see Mount Everest from Khopra Danda?
faqs.a: No. Everest lies about 300 km to the east and is not visible from anywhere in the Annapurna region. From Khopra you see Dhaulagiri I at 8,167 m, Annapurna South at 7,219 m, Fang, Nilgiri, Tukuche Peak and the Dhaulagiri range, which together make one of the finest high mountain panoramas in central Nepal.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit Khopra Danda?
faqs.a: October and November offer the clearest views and stable weather. March and April are next best, with rhododendrons flowering on the lower trail and mostly clear mornings. December to February is cold and quiet, with snow possible on the ridge. June to September is monsoon: wet, cloudy and leech-prone below the pastures, and we do not recommend it.

faqs.q: Is Khopra Danda safe for solo female travellers?
faqs.a: The trail and community lodges have a good safety record, and staff are used to foreign guests. The main risks are navigational and weather-related: the path above Chistibang and Bayeli crosses open pasture that becomes confusing in cloud or snow. We recommend a licensed guide, and solo travellers booking with us get a female guide on request, subject to availability.
